entries.description: The Aamber Pegasus is a home computer designed by Technosys Research Labs. The computer was released in early 1981 in New Zealand for an unknown retail price. The computer was not released outside of New Zealand. The Pegasus sold around only 100 units when it was first released, due to the popularity of Apple II computers. The computers were manufactured until Technosys's collapse in late 1981.

entries.description: The Acorn Archimedes is a family of personal computers designed by Acorn Computers Ltd. The first models were released in June 1987 in Europe at a retail price around £800. The computers were also released in Australia (1988) and in limited availability in North America (1990). The Archimedes computers were one of the most powerful available during the late 1980s and early 1990s. The computers were manufactured until an unspecified time in 1995.

entries.description: The Acorn Atom is a home computer designed by Acorn Computers Ltd. The computer was released in 1980 in Europe at a retail price ranging from £120 to £200, depending on the package bought. The computer was not released outside of Europe. The Atom was Acorn's first computer to be aimed squarely at the home market. The computer was manufactured until an unspecified time in 1983.

models.name: BBC Micro Model A
models.notes: The Model A was the entry-level model, often lacking several expansion ports that were available on the Model B.

models.name: BBC Micro Model B
models.notes: The most common and popular model, known for its extensive connectivity and graphics capabilities. The motherboard was designed to allow upgrades from Model A.

models.name: BBC Micro Model B+64K
models.ram: 64 KB (32KB user RAM + 12KB shadow RAM + 20KB sideways RAM)
models.notes: Extended the life of the BBC Micro, incorporating additional RAM and the WD1770 disc interface as standard.

models.name: BBC Micro Model B+128K
models.notes: Further RAM expansion, building on the B+64K.

entries.description: The Acorn BBC Micro was a series of 8-bit microcomputers developed for the BBC Computer Literacy Project. It was renowned for its robust build, powerful BBC BASIC interpreter, extensive expansion capabilities, and significant impact on education in the UK.
entries.legacy: Pivotal in UK education, inspiring a generation of programmers and fostering computer literacy. Many iconic British computer games and educational software were developed for the platform.
entries.display: 8 modes: 5 graphics, 2 text only and 1 Teletext
entries.media: Cassette tape, Floppy disc, Winchester HD

models.name: Acorn Electron
models.cpu: Synertek SY6502A at 2 MHz (but effectively slower when accessing RAM)
models.notes: The Electron used a custom 'ULA' (Uncommitted Logic Array) chip to integrate many functions found in separate chips on the BBC Micro. This reduced cost but led to slower RAM access and some compatibility issues with BBC Micro software. It lacked the BBC Micro's Teletext Mode 7, 1MHz bus, and dedicated serial/printer ports as standard.

entries.description: The Acorn Electron was an 8-bit home microcomputer designed by Acorn Computers as a lower-cost alternative to the BBC Micro. It aimed to bring the power of BBC BASIC and educational software to a wider home market.
entries.legacy: Despite a troubled launch due to manufacturing issues, the Electron achieved respectable sales, particularly after price drops. It brought computing to many UK homes and was a significant part of the 1980s British home computer boom, often used for games and introductory programming.

models.name: Amstrad CPC 464
models.notes: The initial and most popular model. Its all-in-one approach with a dedicated monitor was a significant advantage over competitors that required a separate TV.

models.name: Amstrad CPC 664
models.notes: A short-lived model, introduced between the 464 and 6128, aiming to provide a built-in floppy drive. It was quickly superseded by the 6128.

models.name: Amstrad CPC 6128
models.launchPrice: £299 (with green monitor), £399 (with color monitor) - UK; US$699 (green), US$799 (color) - US launch
models.notes: The most advanced and commercially successful model in the original CPC line, offering 128KB RAM and built-in floppy drive, making it more suitable for productivity software like CP/M.

models.name: Amstrad CPC 464 Plus
models.cpu: Zilog Z80A at 4 MHz (integrated into ASIC)
models.notes: Part of the 'Plus' range, an attempt to refresh the CPC line with improved graphics/sound and a cartridge slot for instant loading games. Less commercially successful than the original CPCs.

models.name: Amstrad CPC 6128 Plus
models.cpu: Zilog Z80A at 4 MHz (integrated into ASIC)
models.notes: The more powerful model of the 'Plus' range, featuring 128KB RAM and a floppy drive. It also featured a cartridge slot, unlike the original 6128.

entries.description: The Amstrad CPC (Colour Personal Computer) was a series of 8-bit home computers designed as a complete system, bundled with a monitor and integrated storage. It was highly successful in Europe, known for its robust build, ease of use, and competitive pricing, offering a strong alternative to rivals like the Commodore 64 and ZX Spectrum.
entries.legacy: The Amstrad CPC was a significant player in the European home computer market, particularly in the UK, France, Spain, and Germany. It fostered a large user base and a vibrant software development scene, especially for games. Its 'complete system' approach influenced later computer bundles. While less globally recognized than some rivals, it remains a beloved retro computing platform.
entries.media: Compact Cassette (C464, C464 Plus); 3-inch Compact Floppy Disk (C664, C6128, C6128 Plus, also external for C464); ROM Cartridge (Plus series)

models.name: Amstrad CPC 464 Plus
models.launchPrice: Similar to original 464, but for the enhanced features.
models.cpu: Zilog Z80A at 4 MHz (functionality integrated into a custom ASIC chip)
models.notes: Represented the entry-level of the Plus range. Its reliance on cartridges for firmware meant it would not boot without a system cartridge inserted. Lacked the tape counter and the audible loading sounds of the original 464.

models.name: Amstrad CPC 6128 Plus
models.launchPrice: Similar to original 6128, but for the enhanced features.
models.cpu: Zilog Z80A at 4 MHz (functionality integrated into a custom ASIC chip)
models.notes: The more powerful model of the Plus range, offering 128KB RAM and an integrated floppy drive, combining the new hardware enhancements with the greater productivity capabilities of the 6128. It notably removed the cassette port found on the original 6128.

models.name: Amstrad GX4000
models.launchPrice: £99 (console only), £199 (bundle with monitor and Burnin' Rubber)
models.cpu: Zilog Z80A at 4 MHz (integrated into ASIC)
models.notes: Amstrad's attempt to enter the dedicated video game console market using the Plus hardware. It was essentially a CPC 464 Plus motherboard without the keyboard and cassette deck, packaged into a compact console case. It struggled due to a limited software library and competition from 16-bit consoles.

entries.description: The Amstrad CPC Plus range was a late refresh of the highly successful Amstrad CPC 8-bit computer line, launched in 1990. Designed to compete with more advanced 16-bit systems like the Amiga and Atari ST, the Plus models featured significant hardware enhancements, including an expanded color palette, hardware sprites, and a cartridge slot, aiming for a more console-like experience.
entries.legacy: The Amstrad CPC Plus range, while technologically superior to the original CPCs in many aspects, was not as commercially successful. It was released too late into the 8-bit era, facing stiff competition from 16-bit machines (Amiga, Atari ST) and increasingly dominant Japanese consoles. Software support for the new hardware features was limited, as many developers stuck to the original CPC's capabilities for broader compatibility. Despite this, the Plus range represents an interesting evolutionary step for Amstrad and is appreciated by collectors for its advanced features.
entries.media: Compact Cassette (464 Plus); 3-inch Compact Floppy Disk (6128 Plus); ROM Cartridge (primary media for all Plus models and GX4000)

models.name: Amstrad GX4000
models.launchPrice: £99 (console only), £199 (bundle with CM14 monitor, joypad, and 'Burnin' Rubber' cartridge)
models.cpu: Zilog Z80A at 4 MHz (functionality integrated into a custom ASIC chip)
models.notes: The GX4000's hardware was almost identical to the Amstrad CPC Plus computers, primarily differing in its lack of a keyboard and integrated storage drives. Its primary selling point was the enhanced graphics and sound over the original CPCs, aimed at providing a more competitive gaming experience. However, the limited number of games that fully utilized these new features hampered its success.

entries.description: The Amstrad GX4000 was Amstrad's dedicated video game console, released in 1990. It was essentially a stripped-down version of the Amstrad CPC Plus computer hardware, redesigned for the console market. It aimed to compete with 8-bit rivals like the Nintendo Entertainment System and Sega Master System, and even nascent 16-bit systems, but ultimately had limited success due to a small game library and strong competition.
entries.legacy: The Amstrad GX4000 is widely considered a commercial failure for Amstrad. Released at the tail end of the 8-bit era, it struggled to compete against established rivals (NES, Master System) and the emerging 16-bit powerhouses (Mega Drive, Super NES). Its biggest weakness was the extremely limited library of games (around 20-30 official releases), many of which were simply ports of older CPC games that didn't fully leverage the new hardware. Despite its commercial struggles, it's a unique piece of video game history and a collector's item for retro enthusiasts.
entries.media: ROM Cartridge (primary and only medium for games)

models.name: Amstrad PCW8256
models.notes: The launch model of the PCW series, marketed as an all-in-one word processing system. It came bundled with LocoScript and CP/M Plus, making it suitable for both word processing and business software.

models.name: Amstrad PCW8512
models.notes: An enhanced version of the 8256 with more memory and different drive configuration, allowing for more complex CP/M software and larger documents in LocoScript.

models.name: Amstrad PCW9512
models.notes: Featured a redesigned case and bundled a daisy-wheel printer instead of the dot-matrix printer, aiming more at professional users. It was one of the first PCWs to use 3-inch double-sided disks.

models.name: Amstrad PCW9256
models.notes: A cost-reduced version aimed at the home market, still bundled with LocoScript but missing advanced expansion options of earlier PCWs.

models.name: Amstrad PCW10
models.notes: The final PCW model, compact and all-in-one, with a 3.5-inch floppy and modernized case. It was marketed as an affordable word processor but competed poorly with low-end PCs by the 1990s.

entries.description: The Amstrad PCW (Personal Computer Wordprocessor) was a series of Z80-based personal computers designed primarily for word processing but fully capable of running general-purpose software. Bundled with a monitor, printer, and word processing software at an affordable price, it became one of Europe's most popular productivity machines of the late 1980s, especially in small offices and home businesses.
entries.legacy: The Amstrad PCW revolutionized affordable computing for office and home users by offering a complete, ready-to-use word processing system. It sold over 8 million units worldwide, especially in Europe, and introduced many first-time computer users to digital word processing. Its influence extended into small business computing before being overtaken by IBM PC compatibles.
entries.media: 3-inch floppy disks (single- or double-sided); 3.5-inch floppy disks (PCW10 model)

models.name: APF-M1000 / MP1000 (Base Console)
models.cpu: Motorola 6800 (8-bit) at 0.89 MHz (derived from a 3.579 MHz oscillator)
models.notes: Released a year before the full Imagination Machine, the M1000/MP1000 was a standalone second-generation video game console designed to compete with the Atari 2600. It had a built-in game 'Rocket Patrol' and was the foundation upon which the Imagination Machine was built.

models.name: APF Imagination Machine (Full System)
models.launchPrice: US$599 - US$700 (equivalent to approx. US$2,600 - US$3,000 in 2024)
models.ram: 9 KB (expandable to 17 KB with RAM cartridges)
models.notes: The complete Imagination Machine combined the M1000 console (which docked into the IM-1 module) with the keyboard, cassette drive, expanded RAM/ROM, and BASIC interpreter. It was an early pioneer in the hybrid console/computer market.

entries.description: The APF Imagination Machine was an innovative hybrid system, combining the APF-M1000 (or MP1000) video game console with the IM-1 computer component. This modular design allowed users to upgrade from a basic game console to a fully functional home computer, complete with a keyboard, BASIC programming, and integrated tape storage, positioning it as an early attempt to offer both entertainment and productivity in a single package.
entries.legacy: While not a commercial blockbuster, the APF Imagination Machine is historically significant as one of the earliest and most ambitious attempts to converge game consoles and personal computers. It predated similar efforts by Atari (with their never-released 2600 computer add-on) and Commodore (with the VIC-20). Its modularity and focus on user programming were forward-thinking. It fostered an active community of home programmers for a time, but APF Electronics ultimately went out of business during the video game crash of 1983.
entries.media: ROM Cartridges (for games and the BASIC interpreter); Cassette Tapes (for programs, data, and user-created content; featured dual-track for data + audio instructions); 5.25-inch Floppy Disks (optional via Expansion Box and dedicated drive)

models.name: APF MP-1000 (Standard Console)
models.cpu: Motorola 6800 (8-bit) at 0.89 MHz (derived from a 3.579 MHz oscillator)
models.notes: The MP-1000 was a compact, self-contained console. Its primary differentiator was the potential for expansion via a side port, which later became the backbone of the APF Imagination Machine. It was known for its decent graphics for the era and its unique controllers with numeric keypads.

entries.description: The APF MP-1000 was a second-generation home video game console released by APF Electronics, a year prior to its integration into the 'Imagination Machine' hybrid system. It aimed to compete with early cartridge-based consoles like the Atari 2600 and Magnavox Odyssey². It featured a built-in game, 'Rocket Patrol', and utilized an uncommon Motorola 6800 processor.
entries.legacy: The APF MP-1000 is primarily remembered as the base unit for the more ambitious APF Imagination Machine. As a standalone console, it struggled to gain significant market share against the Atari 2600, which had a much larger game library and brand recognition. Its unique controllers and expandability are often highlighted in retro gaming communities. It represents an early, albeit niche, entry into the second generation of video game consoles.

models.name: Apogee BK-01
models.launchPrice: Information not readily available in Western sources, but likely priced for the Soviet domestic market.
models.cpu: KR580VM80A (Soviet clone of Intel 8080) at 1.78 MHz

models.notes: Being based on the 'Radio 86RK', the Apogee BK-01 shared its fundamental architecture, which focused on simplicity and low-cost production. Its text-based nature made it more suited for programming and educational tasks than sophisticated graphics-intensive games, though many text-based and character-graphic games were popular.

models.name: Apogee BK-01C
models.notes: This was an improved version that addressed one of the main limitations of the original BK-01 by adding color output, making it more appealing for games and general home use.

entries.manufacturer: Various factories in the Soviet Union (e.g., Zavod BRA - Завод БРА)
entries.description: The Apogee BK-01 was an 8-bit personal computer widely produced in the Soviet Union. It was a factory-produced version of the popular 'Radio 86RK' design, which was published as a build-it-yourself project in a Soviet radio amateur magazine. This made it a significant entry-level computer for many Soviet citizens, used for basic computing, programming, and simple games.
entries.legacy: The Apogee BK-01, as part of the 'Radio 86RK' family, was highly influential in the Soviet Union. It provided many individuals with their first access to a personal computer, fostering a generation of programmers and enthusiasts. Despite its technical limitations compared to Western counterparts (especially in graphics), a vibrant community developed around it, creating software, games, and hardware modifications. It played a significant role in the 'computerization' efforts in the USSR and post-Soviet states.
entries.media: Compact Cassette Tape (primary storage for programs and data)

models.name: Apple II (Original)
models.notes: The groundbreaking model that established Apple. Known for its iconic beige case and rainbow Apple logo (reflecting its color graphics capabilities). Its open expansion slots fostered a vibrant ecosystem of third-party hardware.

models.name: Apple II Plus
models.ram: 16 KB or 48 KB (standard; expandable to 64 KB with Language Card)
models.notes: An incremental update that made Applesoft BASIC standard in ROM (replacing Integer BASIC) and increased RAM to 48KB. It cemented the Apple II's market position.

models.name: Apple IIe
models.ram: 64 KB (standard, expandable to 1 MB+ with cards)
models.notes: The most popular and longest-lived Apple II model. It significantly lowered costs, reduced chip count, and introduced native 80-column text and lowercase, making many common expansion cards redundant. The 'Enhanced IIe' and 'Platinum IIe' were later revisions.

models.name: Apple IIc
models.notes: Apple's attempt at a portable (though not battery-powered) Apple II, featuring a compact, all-in-one design with a built-in floppy drive and no expansion slots. It was designed to appeal to users who wanted simplicity and portability. The 'IIc Plus' was a later, faster revision.

models.name: Apple IIGS
models.notes: The most advanced and final model in the Apple II series, bridging the gap between 8-bit Apple IIs and the Macintosh. It featured a 16-bit processor, greatly enhanced graphics and sound (often called 'GS' for Graphics and Sound), and a Mac-like graphical user interface (GS/OS). It maintained strong Apple II software compatibility.

entries.description: The Apple II series was a family of 8-bit home computers, beginning with the original Apple II in 1977. Designed by Steve Wozniak, it revolutionized the personal computer market by offering an integrated keyboard, color graphics, and a user-friendly design. Its open architecture with expansion slots allowed for extensive third-party hardware and software development, making it hugely popular in homes, schools, and businesses, particularly with the introduction of the VisiCalc spreadsheet.
entries.legacy: The Apple II's impact on the personal computer revolution is immense. It brought computing to the masses, establishing the home computer as a viable product category. Its success provided the financial foundation for Apple Computer to develop the Macintosh. The Apple II fostered a generation of programmers, designers, and users, influencing countless careers and shaping the future of technology. Its longevity (produced for 16 years) and vast software library solidify its place as a legendary machine in computing history. It's often contrasted with the IBM PC for its focus on integrated color graphics and ease of use, appealing to a different, broader market.
entries.media: Compact Cassette Tape (early models, 1977-1978); 5.25-inch Floppy Disks (140KB, standard from 1978 with Disk II); 3.5-inch Floppy Disks (800KB, later models like IIc, IIGS); Hard Drives (via expansion cards, e.g., Apple ProFile, SCSI drives)

models.name: Apple IIGS (Wozniak/ROM 01)
models.ram: 256 KB (standard, expandable to 1 MB+ via memory expansion slot, up to 8 MB+ with third-party cards)
models.notes: The original release of the IIGS, known as the 'Wozniak' model or ROM 01. It included Steve Wozniak's signature cast into the case. It was revolutionary for bringing Mac-like GUI capabilities and advanced multimedia to the Apple II line.

models.name: Apple IIGS (ROM 03)
models.launchPrice: N/A (replacement for ROM 01, same pricing generally)
models.notes: This revision addressed bugs and improved performance with a larger ROM containing updated system firmware and the AppleTalk networking stack. It became the standard IIGS model sold after 1989.

entries.description: The Apple IIGS (Graphics and Sound) was the most powerful and final model in the Apple II series, bridging the gap between the venerable 8-bit Apple IIs and the Macintosh line. It featured a powerful 16-bit processor, greatly enhanced graphics and sound capabilities, and a Macintosh-like graphical user interface (GS/OS), while maintaining strong backward compatibility with the vast library of Apple II software.
entries.legacy: The Apple IIGS represents the pinnacle of the Apple II line, demonstrating Apple's commitment to the platform even as the Macintosh gained prominence. While it was technologically impressive, its market success was hampered by competition from more powerful and cheaper PCs and Macs, as well as a limited software library that fully utilized its advanced features. Despite this, the IIGS is highly regarded by enthusiasts for its unique blend of 8-bit nostalgia and 16-bit capabilities, and it fostered a loyal community of users and developers who created impressive software for it. It remains a beloved system for retrocomputing, especially for its unique audio capabilities.
entries.media: 3.5-inch Floppy Disks (800KB, standard); 5.25-inch Floppy Disks (140KB, via Disk II or DuoDisk drives); Hard Drives (via SCSI expansion cards); CD-ROM Drives (via SCSI expansion cards)

models.name: Apple III (Original / Sara)
models.ram: 128 KB (standard, expandable up to 256 KB via bank-switching and memory board)
models.notes: Code-named 'Sara' during development. Its initial release was marred by widespread hardware failures, primarily due to Steve Jobs' insistence on a fanless design (leading to overheating and chip dislodgement) and issues with manufacturing 'fineline' circuit boards. Apple reportedly had to replace 14,000 units.

models.name: Apple III Revised
models.notes: This was Apple's attempt to rectify the issues of the original. It featured a redesigned logic board with wider traces, improved chip sockets, and came standard with 256KB RAM. While more reliable, the initial negative reputation was difficult to overcome.

models.name: Apple III Plus
models.notes: The final revision, designed to truly fix all lingering hardware problems and improve user experience. It was a reliable machine, but by its release, the IBM PC dominated the business market, and the Macintosh was on the horizon. It had a very short market life.

entries.description: The Apple III was Apple's first attempt to create a computer specifically for the business market, designed as the successor to the highly successful Apple II. It featured a faster processor, more RAM, built-in disk drive support, and a new operating system (SOS). However, it was plagued by significant hardware defects and design flaws upon its initial release, leading to a poor reputation and limited commercial success despite later revisions.
entries.legacy: The Apple III is widely considered Apple's first major commercial failure. Its initial reliability issues severely damaged its reputation, a blow from which it never fully recovered. Despite later hardware fixes and the advanced nature of its SOS operating system (which later influenced ProDOS for the Apple II), it failed to compete effectively with the burgeoning IBM PC market. The failure of the Apple III ironically led Apple to recommit to the Apple II line, resulting in the highly successful Apple IIe. Today, the Apple III is a rare collector's item, primarily known for its troubled history rather than its technological merits, serving as a reminder of the challenges and risks in early personal computing.
entries.media: 5.25-inch Floppy Disks (140KB, for Disk III drives); Hard Drives (Apple ProFile, 5MB or 10MB external hard drive)

models.name: Macintosh 128K
models.notes: The original 'skinny Mac.' Its revolutionary GUI, iconic compact 'all-in-one' design (dubbed 'the toaster'), and focus on desktop publishing (with the LaserWriter printer) profoundly influenced future computing. However, its limited RAM (128KB) and reliance on a single floppy drive were significant constraints, especially given the memory demands of the GUI. It was soon upgraded to the Macintosh 512K.

entries.description: The original Apple Macintosh was a revolutionary personal computer introduced with a famous Super Bowl advertisement. It was the first commercially successful personal computer to feature a graphical user interface (GUI) and a mouse, rather than a command-line interface. Its 'point-and-click' paradigm, combined with a built-in screen and compact design, aimed to make computing accessible and intuitive for the average person, ushering in a new era of personal computing.
entries.legacy: The original Macintosh was a landmark product that fundamentally changed the personal computer industry. While its initial sales were slow due to cost and limited software, its innovative GUI proved to be the future of computing. It laid the groundwork for all modern operating systems and user interfaces. The Macintosh's focus on ease of use, creativity, and graphical applications (especially desktop publishing) carved out a distinct market. It established Apple's reputation as an innovator and continues to be revered as a design icon and a pivotal moment in computing history.

models.name: MicroBee 16KB / 32KB (Original Kit)
models.notes: Initially sold as a two-board kit in 'Your Computer' magazine. The design was based on existing S-100 bus components. Its success led to pre-built versions and a significant contract with the New South Wales Department of Education.

models.name: MicroBee 32IC / 64K
models.cpu: Zilog Z80A at 2 MHz (some later models possibly faster, e.g., 3.375 MHz)
models.notes: These models introduced larger RAM capacities and refined the core design. They often came in a distinctive two-tone beige and black case. These were popular for school and home use.

models.name: MicroBee Premium 128K / Premium PC85
models.notes: A more advanced model aimed at business and power users. It offered significantly more RAM, faster CPU, improved video output (including basic color), and integrated floppy drive support. It further supported networking options like BeeNet and StarNet.

models.name: MicroBee 256TC / Telecomputer
models.cpu: Zilog Z80A (speed may vary, possibly up to 4MHz)
models.notes: A high-end model for the MicroBee line, incorporating larger RAM, standard twin floppy drives, and more advanced communication features, aiming for a 'telecomputing' workstation. This model likely included CP/M support more prominently.

models.name: MicroBee Matilda (640TC)
models.cpu: Intel 8088 (for PC-XT compatibility) and Zilog Z80 (for backward compatibility)
models.notes: A significant departure, the Matilda was an IBM PC-XT clone with special hardware to provide backward compatibility with the earlier Z80-based MicroBee software. It was an attempt to compete in the rapidly changing market, but it came late and faced technical challenges.

entries.description: The MicroBee was a series of 8-bit home and educational computers designed and manufactured in Australia by Applied Technology. Initially released as a kit in 1982, it gained popularity for its modular design, Z80 processor, and unique video display capabilities. The MicroBee became a staple in Australian schools and homes, playing a key role in the country's early personal computing landscape.
entries.legacy: The MicroBee series holds a cherished place in Australian computing history. It was the first commercially produced personal computer in Australia and became highly influential in schools and homes, nurturing a generation of computer users and programmers. Despite the eventual dominance of international brands like IBM PC, Commodore, and Apple, the MicroBee maintained a loyal following and demonstrated Australia's capacity for innovation in the tech sector. The community around the MicroBee remains active today, with emulators and archives preserving its software and history.
entries.media: Compact Cassette Tape (early models, 300/1200 baud); 5.25-inch Floppy Disks (140KB, for CP/M or proprietary formats); 3.5-inch Floppy Disks (720KB, for later models); Hard Drives (optional, for later, more advanced models)

entries.description: The Apricot PC, launched in 1983 by Apricot Computers Ltd., was a UK-designed personal computer aimed primarily at business and professional users. It featured an Intel 8086 CPU and offered a choice of MS-DOS or CP/M-86 operating systems, making it compatible with popular business software of the time. With graphics and display options comparable to IBM PC standards, as well as support for floppy disks and optional hard drives, the Apricot PC provided a reliable and relatively compact computing solution. It gained popularity in Europe as an alternative to IBM PCs and laid the groundwork for later Apricot models such as the Xi series.

models.name: Arduboy (Original)
models.launchPrice: US$39 - US$49 (Kickstarter price varies by tier)
models.notes: Launched successfully on Kickstarter. The original model established the core concept: a tiny, durable, open-source gaming device. Its firmware and games are written in C++ using the Arduino IDE, making it accessible to those familiar with Arduino programming.

models.name: Arduboy FX
models.notes: An upgraded version that addresses the original's limited storage by adding a 16MB external flash chip. This allows users to store a large library of games on the device, easily switching between them without re-flashing, greatly enhancing its usability.

entries.description: The Arduboy is a credit card-sized, open-source gaming platform built around the Arduino ecosystem. Designed for hobbyists, educators, and retro-gaming enthusiasts, it encourages users to learn coding by creating and sharing their own 8-bit games. Its minimalist design, simple controls, and OLED screen give it a distinct retro aesthetic, while its open-source nature fosters a strong community.
entries.legacy: The Arduboy successfully carved out a niche as an accessible, open-source gaming and development platform. It provided a tangible, physical device for Arduino enthusiasts and aspiring game developers to bring their 8-bit game ideas to life. While not a mainstream gaming console, its educational value and retro appeal have ensured its place in the indie and DIY electronics community, fostering creativity and a love for low-level programming.
entries.media: Internal Flash Memory (for single game on original model); External SPI Flash Memory (16MB on Arduboy FX, for multiple games)

models.name: Atari VCS (Heavy Sixer)
models.notes: The earliest version of the 2600, distinguished by its thick plastic casing and six front switches. Its internal shielding was also heavier. Only produced for about a year before being replaced by cost-reduced versions.

models.name: Atari VCS (Light Sixer)
models.notes: A cost-reduced version of the original, with thinner plastic casing and lighter internal shielding. Functionally identical to the Heavy Sixer, but cheaper to manufacture.

models.name: Atari 2600 (Four Switch)
models.notes: The most common and recognizable version of the Atari 2600. It moved the left and right difficulty switches to the rear of the console, simplifying the front panel. This model dominated the market during the console's peak popularity.

models.name: Atari 2600 Jr.
models.notes: A final, highly cost-reduced redesign released during the Nintendo Entertainment System era. It featured a much smaller, sleeker case with a rainbow stripe, designed to look more like the 7800. It still played all 2600 games and aimed to be an ultra-affordable entry point into gaming.

entries.description: The Atari 2600, originally released as the Atari Video Computer System (VCS), was the console that popularized the use of interchangeable ROM cartridges for video games. Despite its relatively simplistic hardware, its success launched the second generation of video game consoles and transformed the nascent video game industry into a global phenomenon. It remained a dominant force in the market for several years, introducing millions to home video gaming.
entries.legacy: The Atari 2600 is arguably the most influential video game console in history. It revolutionized the entertainment industry, creating the home video game market as we know it. Its immense success, however, also contributed to the video game crash of 1983 due to market oversaturation and quality control issues. Despite this, its impact is undeniable. It introduced concepts like third-party development, licensed properties in games, and hardware revisions. It remains a beloved classic for retro gaming enthusiasts worldwide.
entries.media: ROM Cartridges (proprietary format, ranging from 2KB to 32KB for larger bank-switched games)

models.name: Atari 5200 SuperSystem (4-port)
models.cpu: MOS Technology 6502C (8-bit, custom variant) at 1.79 MHz
models.notes: The initial and most common version. Its large footprint and bulky external power supply were notable. The non-centering analog joysticks were a major point of criticism, as they lacked the tactile feedback needed for many popular action games. Bundled with a special switch box that automatically switched the TV input when the console was powered on.

models.name: Atari 5200 SuperSystem (2-port)
models.launchPrice: US$149.99 (often bundled with a game, e.g., Pac-Man)
models.notes: A cost-reduced revision that removed two joystick ports and swapped the proprietary RF switch box with a standard external power supply. It also moved the start/pause/reset buttons to the front. While more compact, it didn't solve the core controller issues.

entries.description: The Atari 5200 SuperSystem was a second-generation home video game console designed as the successor to the immensely popular Atari 2600. It was essentially an Atari 800 home computer stripped down into a console form factor, leveraging its custom ANTIC, GTIA, and POKEY chips for superior graphics and sound. However, despite its technical prowess, it suffered from a late release, a poorly designed controller, lack of 2600 backward compatibility (initially), and stiff competition, leading to limited commercial success.
entries.legacy: The Atari 5200 is largely considered a commercial failure for Atari, selling just over 1 million units compared to the 2600's millions. Its late entry into the market, problematic controllers, lack of immediate backward compatibility with the 2600's massive library, and the onset of the 1983 video game crash sealed its fate. Despite its technical superiority to many of its contemporaries, it couldn't overcome its design flaws and market conditions. Today, it's a niche collector's item, appreciated by enthusiasts for its powerful hardware and excellent arcade ports, but widely remembered for its missteps.

models.name: Atari 7800 ProSystem
models.launchPrice: US$140 (in 1986, often bundled with Pole Position II)
models.cpu: MOS Technology 6502C (custom variant, dubbed 'MARIA's CPU' when running 7800 games) at 1.79 MHz (PAL) / 1.77 MHz (NTSC) or 1.33 MHz (when running 2600 games)
models.notes: Designed to be highly compatible with the 2600, addressing a major flaw of the 5200. The MARIA graphics chip was a significant improvement, capable of many more colors than its rivals. However, the lack of a dedicated sound chip in the console itself (requiring it on expensive cartridges) limited audio potential for most games.

entries.description: The Atari 7800 ProSystem was a third-generation home video game console initially designed in 1984 as a successor to the ill-fated Atari 5200 and a competitor to the emerging Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) and Sega Master System. Its key features included native backward compatibility with the hugely popular Atari 2600, significantly improved graphics capabilities (via the MARIA chip), and better-designed digital controllers. Although technically superior to its predecessor and robustly built, its delayed mass release and the established dominance of Nintendo limited its commercial success.
entries.legacy: The Atari 7800 was a console with potential that arrived too late to reclaim Atari's dominance. Its initial delay (due to Atari's sale from Warner Communications to Jack Tramiel) allowed Nintendo to firmly establish the NES in the market. While technically capable, the console suffered from a limited software library (especially new 7800-exclusive titles), a lack of first-party support from a struggling Atari Corp., and the absence of a dedicated, powerful sound chip on the console itself. It's remembered as Atari's last major effort in the console wars of the 1980s, a system that, had it been released earlier with more robust sound and software backing, might have significantly altered video game history. Today, it is appreciated by retro collectors for its excellent arcade ports and 2600 compatibility.

models.name: Atari 800

entries.description: The Atari 800 was a high-end 8-bit home computer released alongside its more affordable sibling, the Atari 400. Designed with a focus on advanced multimedia capabilities through its custom chipset (ANTIC, GTIA, POKEY), it featured superior graphics and sound compared to many contemporaries. It was marketed as a complete home computer system, suitable for gaming, education, and general computing, and was notable for its robust construction and user-friendly modular expansion.
entries.legacy: The Atari 800, along with the Atari 400, played a crucial role in the early home computer revolution. While initially overshadowed by the Apple II in some markets, its superior graphics and sound capabilities made it a favorite among gamers and programmers who pushed its multimedia limits. It fostered a vibrant community and a rich library of software, particularly games. Despite its eventual decline due to competition from more affordable and later, more powerful machines (like the Commodore 64 and IBM PC), the Atari 8-bit line left an indelible mark on computing, influencing later systems and maintaining a passionate retrocomputing following. It is recognized for its innovative hardware architecture.

models.notes: The '64-bit' claim was controversial; while its custom chips processed data in 64-bit chunks, its main CPU was a 16-bit 68000. Its complex architecture made it difficult for developers to program, leading to a small and often underwhelming software library that didn't fully exploit its potential.

entries.description: The Atari Jaguar was marketed as the 'world's first 64-bit interactive multimedia system,' developed by Atari Corporation to challenge the dominance of Sega and Nintendo in the console market. It featured a complex multi-chip architecture designed to deliver cutting-edge graphics and sound. Despite its technical ambition and a strong launch marketing campaign, the Jaguar struggled due to its challenging development environment, limited and often low-quality software library, and the impending arrival of true 3D consoles from Sony and Sega, leading to its commercial failure.
entries.legacy: The Atari Jaguar was a commercial failure, selling only around 250,000 units before being discontinued in 1996. It suffered from a severe lack of quality software due to its programming complexity, poor third-party support, and fierce competition from the established Sega Genesis/SNES and the rapidly emerging PlayStation and Sega Saturn. It marked Atari's last foray into the home console market. Despite its shortcomings, it remains an intriguing piece of video game history, notable for its ambitious hardware, unique controller, and a small, dedicated fanbase that continues to develop homebrew titles.

models.name: Atari Jaguar CD
models.cpu: Relies on the Atari Jaguar's Motorola 68000 (13.29 MHz) and custom 'Tom' and 'Jerry' chips. It includes its own dedicated DSP for CD audio.
models.ram: 2 MB DRAM (shares Jaguar's main RAM) + additional RAM within the CD unit itself (specific amount less clear, but contributed to overall system memory).
models.notes: The Jaguar CD featured a double-speed (2x) CD-ROM drive. It also included the 'Virtual Light Machine' (VLM) by Jeff Minter, which generated a unique, psychedelic light show when playing audio CDs. The proprietary CD format allowed for slightly more storage (up to 790MB) than standard CD-ROMs of the time but lacked robust error correction.

entries.description: The Atari Jaguar CD is a CD-ROM peripheral designed for the Atari Jaguar console. Released in late 1995, it aimed to provide greatly expanded storage capacity for games, allowing for full-motion video (FMV), larger game worlds, and CD-quality audio, features that were increasingly expected by consumers. Its unique design, which clipped onto the top of the Jaguar console, was distinctive but often criticized for its 'toilet bowl' appearance. Despite its technical enhancements, it suffered from the Jaguar's underlying issues, including a small user base and a lack of compelling software.
entries.legacy: The Atari Jaguar CD was a commercial failure, selling fewer than 20,000 units. Its late release (nearly two years after the base Jaguar), alongside the ongoing struggles of the Jaguar console itself, meant it entered a market already being revolutionized by the Sony PlayStation and Sega Saturn, both of which had integrated CD-ROM drives and superior 3D capabilities. The limited software library (only around 13-20 official titles) and the add-on's somewhat unusual design further hampered its appeal. It represents one of Atari's final attempts to remain relevant in the console market, but ultimately it became a footnote in the history of add-ons and a rare collector's item.
entries.media: CD-ROM (proprietary format, up to 790 MB); Memory Track Cartridge (for save data)

models.name: Atari Lynx (Model I)
models.notes: Original large form factor. Known for its advanced graphics and sound, but also its large size and extremely poor battery life (requiring 6 AA batteries for approx. 4-5 hours of play). The ambidextrous design (allowing the screen to be flipped 180 degrees) was unique. Packaged with the game 'California Games'.

models.name: Atari Lynx II
models.notes: A redesigned, more compact, and lighter version of the Lynx I. It addressed some of the original's criticisms by improving ergonomics, slightly improving battery life (though still poor), adding stereo sound to the headphone jack, and incorporating a sleep mode. This was the most common version.

entries.description: The Atari Lynx was a revolutionary handheld game console that debuted as the first portable gaming system with a color LCD screen. Developed by Epyx (originally as the 'Handy'), it boasted advanced graphics capabilities for a handheld, including hardware scaling and distortion, which enabled impressive pseudo-3D effects. Its ergonomic design, ambidextrous controls, and ability to network with other Lynxes via ComLynx were highly innovative. However, its high price, poor battery life, and the overwhelming success of the monochromatic Nintendo Game Boy ultimately limited its commercial viability.
entries.legacy: The Atari Lynx is widely regarded as a technological marvel that was ahead of its time. However, it failed commercially against the Nintendo Game Boy, which offered a lower price point, vastly superior battery life, and a killer app (Tetris), despite its monochrome screen. The Lynx's high cost, large size, and especially its terrible battery life were significant deterrents. Atari's own financial struggles and limited third-party support also hindered its success. Today, the Lynx is a beloved cult classic among retro gaming enthusiasts, admired for its technical ambition and unique game library, proving that technological superiority doesn't always guarantee market success.

models.name: Atari 1040STF / 1040STFM
models.notes: The first 'Mega-Byte' computer to break the $1000 price barrier, making 1MB of RAM and a built-in floppy drive affordable. This was the most popular and influential ST model, solidifying its place in the market.

models.name: Atari Mega ST
models.ram: 1 MB, 2 MB, or 4 MB DRAM (user upgradeable)
models.notes: A more professional and expandable version of the ST, featuring a separate keyboard and a beefier case. Aimed at business and power users. Often bundled with a Megafile hard drive.

models.name: Atari STacy
models.launchPrice: US$1,999 (1MB RAM model, approx. US$4,400 in 2025)
models.notes: Atari's first laptop computer. Powered by 12 C-cell batteries (often problematic), or an AC adapter. Featured a monochrome LCD. It was quite bulky and heavy, but offered full ST compatibility on the go.

models.notes: The 'E' stands for 'Enhanced'. This model offered significant improvements in graphics (4096 color palette, blitter) and sound (DMA-driven stereo sound). It was compatible with most ST software and widely popular.

models.cpu: Motorola 68000 (user switchable to 16 MHz) or 68030 (upgrade option)
models.notes: A hybrid between the STE and the TT, offering STE enhancements in a professional desktop case. Featured a faster, switchable 68000 CPU and optional 68030 upgrade, making it a very capable machine for its time. Often considered the ultimate 68000-based ST.

models.name: Atari ST Book
models.launchPrice: US$799 (estimated, very limited release, approx. US$1,700 in 2025)
models.notes: An extremely rare, highly portable notebook computer version of the ST, resembling modern laptops. It was very expensive to produce and had a very limited release, primarily in Europe. A true collector's item.

entries.description: The Atari ST (Sixteen/Thirty-two, referring to its 16-bit external bus and 32-bit internal architecture) was a groundbreaking line of personal computers. It was one of the first home computers to feature a bit-mapped graphical user interface (GUI) in color, using Digital Research's GEM (Graphics Environment Manager) bundled with Atari's own TOS (The Operating System) in ROM. Its fast Motorola 68000 CPU and, crucially, built-in MIDI ports made it highly popular for desktop publishing and a de facto standard in music production for many years. It was a fierce competitor to the Commodore Amiga and Apple Macintosh.
entries.legacy: The Atari ST played a pivotal role in the personal computer market of the late 1980s. It was particularly successful in Europe (especially Germany and the UK) and significantly impacted the music industry, where its integrated MIDI ports made it indispensable for musicians and studios. While it eventually lost market share to the PC (running Windows) and Amiga, its contributions to GUI computing and music technology are undeniable. It remains a beloved retro computer with a dedicated enthusiast community that continues to develop software, hardware, and operating system enhancements.

Without the keyboard, it booted directly into 'Missile Command'. With the keyboard attached, it booted into Atari BASIC, functioning as a full computer.

entries.description: The Atari XE Game System (XEGS) was a hybrid home computer and video game console, released by Atari Corporation in an effort to capitalize on the booming console market after the 1983 video game crash. It was essentially a repackaged Atari 65XE 8-bit home computer, designed to look more like a console, but retaining full compatibility with the extensive Atari 8-bit computer software and peripherals. It was marketed as a direct competitor to the Nintendo Entertainment System and Sega Master System, offering a unique proposition of being both a game machine and an expandable computer.
entries.legacy: The Atari XEGS was a peculiar product of its time. While technically versatile and backward compatible with a massive software library, it struggled to find its place in a console market dominated by Nintendo. Consumers largely preferred dedicated, simpler game consoles. Atari's marketing was confusing, trying to position it as both a computer and a console. It sold poorly (estimated around 100,000 units) and was discontinued in 1992. Today, it is primarily a collector's item, representing Atari's innovative but ultimately unsuccessful attempt to bridge the gap between home computers and dedicated video game consoles, and a testament to the enduring appeal of the Atari 8-bit computer line.

models.notes: The final, and most common, name for the console after Bally sold the rights to Astrovision. Astrovision tried to promote it more as a computer system, offering an external keyboard and the AstroBASIC cartridge. The console itself remained largely unchanged internally.

entries.description: The Bally Astrocade was a technologically ambitious home video game console, originally designed by Midway, Bally's arcade division. It was noteworthy for its powerful graphics capabilities for its era, including a flexible color palette and hardware-assisted pixel manipulation, which allowed for more detailed visuals than many contemporaries. Its unique controller, built-in games (Gunfight, Checkmate, Calculator, Scribbling), and optional BASIC programming cartridge also set it apart. However, its delayed retail release, challenging hardware to program for, and a fragmented marketing strategy under different names ultimately limited its market impact.
entries.legacy: The Bally Astrocade, despite its technical merits, was a commercial disappointment. Its convoluted release strategy, shifting names, and poor marketing meant it never gained significant traction against the Atari 2600. Developers found its complex hardware challenging to program, leading to a limited library of games that often didn't showcase its full potential. Production effectively ceased in 1983 (though some units were sold until 1984). Today, the Astrocade is a rare and highly sought-after collector's item, particularly among those who appreciate its unique hardware and its place as a technologically advanced, albeit commercially unsuccessful, console of the second generation.

Its primary draw was the novelty of scanning everyday items to influence gameplay. It was often sold in bundles with a game and a set of custom barcodes.

entries.description: The Bandai Datach was a unique handheld gaming device released exclusively in Japan. Its defining feature was a built-in barcode scanner, allowing players to scan real-world barcodes from various products (food, toys, etc.) to generate in-game characters, items, or power-ups. This innovative 'barcode battle' concept aimed to merge physical interaction with digital gameplay. While technologically interesting, its reliance on scanning everyday products for game mechanics, limited software library, and short lifespan prevented it from becoming a major success.
entries.legacy: The Bandai Datach was a commercial failure, largely due to its niche gameplay mechanic, a limited and often repetitive game library (only around 10-15 titles), and the inherent awkwardness of constantly scanning barcodes during gameplay. It was released during the height of the Game Boy's popularity and couldn't compete. However, it is significant as an early, ambitious attempt to bridge physical and digital play. Its concept influenced later barcode-scanning toys and games, including Bandai's own 'Digimon' handhelds (which used contact points on Digivices rather than barcodes) and arcade machines like 'Barcode Battler'. Today, it's a rare and interesting curiosity for collectors of unique and experimental gaming hardware.

entries.description: The Bandai RX-78 was an 8-bit home computer released by Bandai in Japan. While sharing its numerical designation with the iconic Gundam mobile suit, it was a general-purpose computer primarily marketed towards gaming, featuring two joystick ports and a strong emphasis on game cartridges. It launched into a highly competitive Japanese market, notably in the same month as Nintendo's Famicom, which ultimately overshadowed it. Despite its obscurity outside of Japan, it represented Bandai's attempt to enter the home computer market, building on their experience in toys and electronic games.
entries.legacy: The Bandai RX-78 was a commercial failure. Its release in July 1983 coincided directly with the launch of the Nintendo Famicom, which rapidly dominated the Japanese home gaming market. Bandai lacked the software development capacity and marketing power to compete with Nintendo or the established Japanese computer manufacturers like NEC and Sharp. Its game library was small, and many titles are now extremely rare and expensive. Today, the Bandai RX-78 is a highly sought-after collector's item due to its rarity and its place as a unique, albeit unsuccessful, entry in Bandai's diverse history of electronics and gaming.

models.notes: Designed to look like a small arcade cabinet control panel. This model focused on Namco arcade classics. Often battery-powered, but could use an AC adapter. The 'joystick' was a small, integrated digital stick.

models.name: Bandai Let's TV Play Classic: Space Invaders
models.notes: Another popular entry, focusing on Taito's classic shooter. The physical design of the unit would often reflect the game's theme.

models.name: Bandai Let's TV Play Classic: Dragon Ball Z (and other licensed titles)
models.notes: Bandai also produced units based on their popular licensed franchises (e.g., Dragon Ball Z, Ultraman, Kamen Rider), which often featured simpler graphics and gameplay more akin to 8-bit console games rather than arcade perfect emulation. These typically had unique controller designs relevant to the IP.

entries.description: The Bandai Let's TV Play Classic (TV Plug-In Series in the West) was a line of dedicated, plug-and-play video game consoles released by Bandai. Each unit was designed to emulate a specific classic arcade game or series, packaging the hardware, software, and sometimes unique controllers directly into a single unit that plugged directly into a television's A/V input. They were a direct competitor to similar 'TV Game' or 'Plug & Play' devices from companies like Jakks Pacific (known for their 'TV Games' line), offering a nostalgic and convenient way to play arcade classics at home without needing a traditional console.
entries.legacy: The Bandai Let's TV Play Classic series, and similar plug-and-play devices from other companies, enjoyed moderate success by tapping into the nostalgia for classic arcade games and offering a convenient, affordable solution. While not revolutionary in terms of technology (they often used System-on-a-Chip emulation), they played a role in popularizing retro gaming and the concept of dedicated mini-consoles. They were precursors to later, more advanced mini-consoles like the NES Classic Edition or PlayStation Classic. The series cemented Bandai's presence in the casual gaming and nostalgia markets.

models.name: Bandai Sufami Turbo (SFT-0100JP)
models.launchPrice: ¥3,980 (Japanese Yen, approximately US$46 at 1996 exchange rates, equivalent to approx. US$92 in 2025)
models.cpu: Relies on the Super Famicom's Ricoh 5A22 (16-bit) at 3.58 MHz (or 2.68 MHz / 1.79 MHz). The Sufami Turbo unit itself contains minimal additional processing for cartridge communication.
models.ram: Uses the Super Famicom's main RAM (128 KB DRAM). Sufami Turbo cartridges contained their own ROM and sometimes a small amount of SRAM for saves.
models.notes: The unit itself did not contain significant processing power but acted as an adapter and a dual-cartridge reader. It allowed for a more affordable cartridge manufacturing process for Bandai. It often came bundled with a game.

entries.description: The Bandai Sufami Turbo was a unique peripheral for Nintendo's Super Famicom (Super Nintendo Entertainment System in the West), released exclusively in Japan. It was designed to allow Bandai to produce and sell Super Famicom games using smaller, cheaper cartridges, bypassing Nintendo's more expensive cartridge manufacturing process. Its most innovative feature was having two cartridge slots, allowing players to insert two Sufami Turbo cartridges simultaneously. This enabled a 'linking' feature where data could be shared between games, often used for cross-game character transfers or expanded content within a series.
entries.legacy: The Bandai Sufami Turbo was a commercial failure, selling poorly during its short lifespan. Only 13 games were officially released, most of which were part of a series intended to utilize the linking feature. It was released late in the Super Famicom's life cycle (1996), at a time when the market was rapidly shifting to 3D consoles like the Nintendo 64, PlayStation, and Sega Saturn. Its niche concept and limited software library failed to capture widespread interest. Today, the Sufami Turbo is a highly sought-after collector's item due to its rarity, unique concept, and its place as an interesting footnote in the history of SNES peripherals and Bandai's attempts at hardware innovation.

Marketed primarily at children, the Super Note Club family combined diary/note/word-processor features with cartridge games and themed educational software, and offered accessories such as a small thermal printer and an illustration scanner.
entries.legacy: A niche but well-remembered line of Bandai edu/toy devices in Japan. It demonstrates Bandai's 1990s strategy of hybrid toy/computer products — collectible today among retro-toy and Bandai enthusiasts.

Its design was somewhat reminiscent of the Intellivision controllers, though developed independently. The system came bundled with the game 'Missile Vader'.

entries.description: The Bandai Super Vision 8000 was a second-generation home video game console released by Bandai exclusively in Japan. It was a pivotal product for Bandai, as it was their first console to utilize a microprocessor (an 8-bit Z80 clone) and ROM cartridges for games, moving beyond the dedicated logic circuits of their earlier 'TV Jack' series. Despite its technological leap and relatively advanced features for its time (such as arcade-style graphics and sound from the AY-3-8910 chip), its high price and a very limited game library ultimately led to its commercial failure.
entries.legacy: The Bandai Super Vision 8000 was a commercial failure, selling very few units and being discontinued in 1982. Its high price point (especially compared to the Atari 2600 in international markets) and extremely limited game library (only 7 titles were ever released) meant it could not compete effectively in the burgeoning console market. Despite its advanced technical specifications for its time, it struggled to attract developers or consumers. Today, the Super Vision 8000 is an extremely rare and highly sought-after collector's item, representing an interesting, albeit short-lived, chapter in Bandai's hardware development and the early history of Japanese video game consoles.

entries.description: The Bandai WonderSwan was a handheld game console released exclusively in Japan. Designed by Gunpei Yokoi's Koto Laboratory (following his departure from Nintendo), it aimed to compete with Nintendo's Game Boy line by offering a lower price, extended battery life, and unique gameplay mechanics. Its most distinctive feature was the ability to play games in both horizontal (landscape) and vertical (portrait) orientations, achieved through two sets of directional pads. While it garnered a respectable market share in Japan and attracted strong third-party support (including Square Enix), it struggled against the overwhelming dominance of the Game Boy and its successor, the Game Boy Color and Game Boy Advance.
entries.legacy: Despite its innovative features and strong backing from Bandai and key developers like Square Enix, the WonderSwan ultimately failed to unseat Nintendo's dominance in the handheld market. Combined sales for all three models reached around 3.5 million units, a respectable number for a challenger but far from the Game Boy's immense success. It is remembered as a well-designed, unique, and technically capable handheld that arrived too late to capture significant market share against the Nintendo 64 and PlayStation-era consoles and then the Game Boy Advance. Today, the WonderSwan is a popular and highly regarded collector's item due to its unique features, strong exclusive game library (especially the Square Enix RPGs), and its historical significance as Gunpei Yokoi's final console.

models.launchPrice: ¥6,800 (Japanese Yen, approximately US$60 at 2000 exchange rates, equivalent to approx. US$100 in 2025)

models.notes: The WonderSwan Color significantly improved upon the original with its color display and increased RAM, making more visually complex games possible. It was backward compatible with monochrome WonderSwan games. It came in various vibrant casing colors, including transparent 'Crystal' versions. Battery life was still impressive at around 20 hours on a single AA battery.

entries.description: The Bandai WonderSwan Color was the successor to the original monochrome WonderSwan, released exclusively in Japan. Designed by Gunpei Yokoi's Koto Laboratory, its primary upgrade was the introduction of a color FSTN reflective LCD screen, making it a direct competitor to Nintendo's Game Boy Color. It retained the unique dual-orientation gameplay (horizontal and vertical) and boasted excellent battery life. The WonderSwan Color gained significant traction by attracting major third-party developers like Square Enix, which released exclusive color remakes of classic Final Fantasy titles for the platform, helping it carve out a respectable, albeit ultimately small, slice of the highly competitive Japanese handheld market.
entries.legacy: The Bandai WonderSwan Color was a valiant attempt by Bandai to compete in the color handheld market dominated by Nintendo. While it offered compelling features like dual orientation and impressive battery life, and secured a strong lineup of exclusive games (especially RPGs from Square Enix), it ultimately could not overcome Nintendo's massive market share, brand recognition, and extensive software library. Its sales, combined with the original WonderSwan and SwanCrystal, reached approximately 3.5 million units. Despite its commercial struggles, the WonderSwan Color is highly regarded by retro gaming enthusiasts and collectors for its unique design, innovative features, and the high quality of many of its exclusive titles. It stands as an important, albeit niche, chapter in the history of handheld gaming, showcasing the vision of Gunpei Yokoi outside of Nintendo.

models.name: Pocket Challenge V2
models.launchPrice: Not sold retail; included as part of Benesse's Shinkenzemi course subscription. Equivalent value would be difficult to ascertain, but the cost was absorbed into tuition.

models.notes: The device's hardware is extremely similar to the WonderSwan Color/SwanCrystal, indicating a shared design lineage, likely from Koto Laboratory. Its cartridges are physically similar to WonderSwan cartridges but are not directly interchangeable due to a different keying on the slot and possibly different electrical pinouts, though some users have found ways to mod systems/carts for compatibility. The V2 designation refers to 'Version 2' within Benesse's Pocket Challenge line, succeeding earlier monochrome versions.

entries.description: The Benesse Pocket Challenge V2 is a handheld educational device designed for students enrolled in Benesse's 'Shinkenzemi' correspondence courses in Japan. While primarily an educational tool for subjects like English, math, science, and social studies, it is notable for its hardware's striking resemblance and **near-perfect compatibility with Bandai's WonderSwan Color**. This unofficial compatibility (cartridges for one often work on the other, though with potential control or display quirks) stems from the fact that it was likely developed by Koto Laboratory (Gunpei Yokoi's company), which also designed the WonderSwan. It served as a digital learning platform with interactive exercises, quizzes, and some game-like elements to engage students.
entries.legacy: The Benesse Pocket Challenge V2 is a fascinating footnote in handheld gaming history due to its direct link to the WonderSwan's hardware. While not a commercial game console, it provided a platform for Bandai/Koto Laboratory's technology to be used in an educational context, extending the life and reach of the WonderSwan architecture. Its existence is a curiosity for collectors interested in the WonderSwan's lineage and obscure Japanese hardware. It demonstrates how handheld technology could be repurposed for specific educational needs, often with hardware very similar to general entertainment devices. For Benesse, it was part of their ongoing strategy to integrate technology into their learning programs, evolving from earlier pen-and-paper or TV-based learning to more interactive portable devices.
entries.media: ROM Cartridges (proprietary format for Benesse's educational software). These cartridges contained specific lessons, exercises, and mini-games.

entries.description: The Benesse Pocket Challenge W is an educational handheld console released in Japan around 2001. It is designed for children to practice math, logic, and other learning skills through interactive games and exercises.
entries.legacy: The Benesse Pocket Challenge W is remembered as a niche educational handheld in Japan. Its impact was limited due to its specialized focus, but it represents the early 2000s trend of merging gaming with learning for young audiences.

models.launchPrice: Information on its original price is scarce due to its primary distribution in Asian markets and its clone nature. Likely competitive with similar home computers of the era, potentially around…
models.notes: The BIT 90's design featured a compact, all-in-one unit with a keyboard. Its use of the Z80 CPU and TMS9918A VDC made it technically similar to MSX computers and the ColecoVision, enabling its partial compatibility with ColecoVision games. This compatibility, however, was not 100% reliable due to variations in BIOS and specific game coding.

entries.description: The Bit Corporation BIT 90 was a home computer system released by the Taiwanese company Bit Corporation in 1983. While marketed as a home computer, it had strong gaming capabilities and is particularly notable for its **partial compatibility with ColecoVision games**, allowing it to play a subset of titles developed for that popular North American console. This made it one of many 'cloned' or compatible systems produced in Asia during the 8-bit era. It offered a Z80 CPU, dedicated video and sound chips, and a cassette tape drive for storage, along with a built-in keyboard.
entries.legacy: The Bit Corporation BIT 90, like many Taiwanese clones of its era, had a limited impact outside of specific regional markets. Its commercial success was hindered by the rise of more prominent and well-supported consoles like the Famicom/NES and by the general decline of standalone home computers in the mid-1980s as dedicated game consoles became dominant. Information on its exact sales figures and impact is scarce. Today, the BIT 90 is a rare and sought-after curiosity for collectors of obscure retro computers and clone systems, particularly those interested in the history of ColecoVision compatibility and Taiwanese hardware development. It represents a fascinating period of intense competition and technological borrowing in the early days of personal computing and home gaming.

models.name: Cambridge Z88
models.launchPrice: £249.95 GBP (approximately US$400 at 1987 exchange rates, equivalent to approx. US$1,100 in 2025)
models.ram: 32 KB internal pseudo-static RAM (expandable up to 3.5 MB via card slots)
models.notes: The Z88 was groundbreaking for its portability, instant-on functionality (no boot-up time), and long battery life (around 20 hours on AA batteries). Its silent keyboard was also a distinct feature. The OZ operating system supported basic multitasking and a 'notebook' metaphor for file management.

entries.manufacturer: Cambridge Computer Ltd. (founded by Sir Clive Sinclair)
entries.description: The Cambridge Z88 was a pioneering portable Zilog Z80-based notebook computer. Designed by Sir Clive Sinclair, it was notable for its extremely lightweight (under 1 kg), silent membrane keyboard, multi-tasking operating system (OZ), and impressive battery life on standard AA batteries. It was conceived as a 'personal electronic notebook' for professionals and students, offering built-in applications like a word processor, spreadsheet, and diary, along with expandability via solid-state memory cards. While not a dedicated gaming machine, its open architecture allowed for simple games and programming.
entries.legacy: The Cambridge Z88, while not a commercial blockbuster, is highly regarded as a visionary product and a precursor to modern notebook and netbook computers. It was ahead of its time in terms of portability, instant-on capability, and battery endurance. Its design philosophy influenced later portable devices. It cemented Sir Clive Sinclair's reputation as an innovator, even after the sale of Sinclair Research. Today, the Z88 enjoys a dedicated cult following among retro computing enthusiasts, who appreciate its unique design, robust build quality, and the ability to still be productive with it using modern connectivity solutions (like SD card interfaces). It stands as a significant milestone in the evolution of portable computing, demonstrating what could be achieved with efficient hardware and clever software design in the 8-bit era.

entries.description: The Camputers Lynx was an 8-bit British home computer known for its relatively advanced graphics capabilities for its time, including high-resolution color graphics. It was released in several configurations (48KB, 96KB, 128KB, and later expandable to 192KB) and aimed to compete directly with popular machines like the Sinclair ZX Spectrum. Despite its technical prowess, including a Z80A CPU and a Motorola 6845 video controller, the Lynx suffered from a high price point, manufacturing issues, and a lack of a robust software library, leading to the company's swift demise.
entries.legacy: The Camputers Lynx is largely remembered as a commercial failure in the highly competitive British home computer market. Despite its strong technical specifications, it was severely hampered by its high price, delays in release, and a tiny software library. Camputers ceased trading in June 1984, just over a year after the Lynx's launch, with only an estimated 30,000 units sold worldwide. Its legacy is one of 'what could have been' – a technically capable machine that succumbed to fierce competition and poor market timing. Today, the Lynx is a rare and highly sought-after collector's item, valued for its unique place in British computing history and its advanced graphical capabilities for an 8-bit machine.

entries.description: The Canon X-07 was a sophisticated handheld computer (often called a 'laptop' or 'notebook' for its era) released by Canon. It was designed as a portable personal computing device for professionals and enthusiasts. Featuring a Z80-compatible CPU and Microsoft BASIC in ROM, it offered programmability and built-in applications. Its unique design included a small, integrated display and a relatively comprehensive keyboard, with the ability to connect to external peripherals like printers and a monitor for a more desktop-like experience.
entries.legacy: The Canon X-07 was part of a wave of early portable computers, attempting to define a new category between calculators, personal organizers, and full-sized desktop machines. While innovative for its time, it faced challenges from rapid technological advancements and competition from more robust laptops or cheaper, more gaming-focused handhelds. Its impact was primarily in the niche market of professionals and enthusiasts who needed portability before the widespread adoption of full-sized laptops. Today, the Canon X-07 is a rare and unique collector's item, primarily appealing to those interested in the history of portable computing, early Z80-based machines, and Canon's less-known ventures into electronics beyond cameras.

entries.description: The Casio Loopy was a 32-bit home video game console released exclusively in Japan. Its defining characteristic was its marketing: it was specifically targeted at young female gamers. To cater to this demographic, the Loopy featured a built-in thermal color printer that allowed users to print stickers from game screenshots, a feature integral to almost every game released for the system. Despite its unique approach and innovation in targeting a new demographic, it faced overwhelming competition from established console giants and ultimately saw a very limited release and a tiny software library.
entries.legacy: The Casio Loopy is a significant but commercially unsuccessful console. Its attempt to carve out a niche by targeting a specific gender and integrating a unique hardware feature was innovative. However, its very limited game library (only 11 titles including the Magical Shop peripheral), high price, and competition from PlayStation and Sega Saturn led to rapid discontinuation in October 1996. Total sales were very low, making it a rare and highly sought-after collector's item today.

entries.description: The Casio PV-1000 was an 8-bit home video game console released exclusively in Japan by Casio. It was Casio's first attempt to enter the dedicated video game console market. Despite a relatively competitive price and hardware architecture somewhat similar to the popular ColecoVision (using a Z80 CPU and a Texas Instruments VDP), the PV-1000 was a commercial failure. It was released at a time when the Nintendo Famicom and Sega SG-1000 were already establishing dominance, leading to its very brief market presence and an extremely limited game library.
entries.legacy: The Casio PV-1000 is remembered for its rarity and its status as a notable failed console. Released alongside the Nintendo Famicom and Sega SG-1000, it was quickly overshadowed. Only 13 official titles were released before its discontinuation in early 1984. It remains a fascinating relic from the competitive early 8-bit era.

entries.description: The Casio PV-2000 was an 8-bit home computer released by Casio in Japan. It was launched simultaneously with the PV-1000 console, but was intended as a more versatile home computer, featuring an integrated keyboard and a BASIC interpreter. While it shared some hardware similarities (like the Z80-compatible CPU and a TI TMS9918A VDP) with other systems of its era, including the MSX standard and ColecoVision, it used a proprietary operating system (C83-BASIC) and incompatible cartridge format, limiting its software ecosystem. It was quickly overshadowed by the booming MSX platform and Nintendo's Famicom, leading to its rapid discontinuation.
entries.legacy: The Casio PV-2000 is primarily known among retro computer enthusiasts and collectors for its extreme rarity and its brief, almost forgotten, existence. It was a victim of terrible market timing. Released just as the MSX standard was gaining momentum (which Casio themselves would soon embrace with the PV-7/16/etc. models) and Nintendo's Famicom was exploding, the PV-2000 had no room to breathe. Its proprietary software format and the unfortunate confusion caused by the PV-1000's incompatible cartridge slot further doomed it. Casio swiftly abandoned the PV-2000, pivoting to become a major MSX manufacturer. Today, it serves as a stark reminder of the intense competition in the 8-bit home computer market in early 1980s Japan, where many technically competent machines failed to find their footing against more dominant platforms.

entries.description: The CCE MC-1000 was an 8-bit home computer developed and released by the Brazilian electronics company CCE. It was equipped with a Zilog Z80A CPU and a Motorola MC6847 video controller, similar to the TRS-80 Color Computer. Notably, its BASIC dialect was very similar to Applesoft BASIC from the Apple II, including specific commands. However, unlike many Brazilian computers of the era which were direct clones of popular foreign models (like the Apple II, ZX Spectrum, or MSX), the MC-1000 had a less clear lineage, possibly being based on the obscure Belgian GEM 1000 or the Hong Kong-made Rabbit RX83. It aimed to be a low-cost personal computer but faced stiff competition from more capable and software-rich machines like the TK-90X and MSX computers that launched around the same time, leading to its limited success and short production run.
entries.legacy: The CCE MC-1000 is an iconic, albeit commercially limited, piece of Brazilian retrocomputing history. Its attempt to establish a unique identity in a market of clones, combined with its 1985 release into a fiercely competitive landscape (including the highly successful MSX standard and the ZX Spectrum clones), sealed its fate. It was discontinued around 1986. Due to its limited sales and unique nature, it is now a highly sought-after collector's item in Brazil. Its legacy lies in representing a specific period of Brazilian industrial policy (the 'reserva de mercado' which protected local production) and the creative attempts by local companies like CCE to provide affordable personal computers, even if they couldn't always compete with international standards in terms of software availability.
